questions.question: Explain the role of decomposers in an ecosystem, the conditions they need, and why the centre of a compost heap becomes hot.
questions.expected_answer: Decomposers, mainly bacteria and fungi, release enzymes onto dead plants, animals and dung, break the complex substances down and absorb them. Their respiration returns carbon dioxide to the air for photosynthesis, and the breakdown releases minerals such as nitrates and phosphates into the soil for plant roots, so nutrients are recycled; without them dead material would pile up and soil would run out of minerals. They need moisture, warmth, oxygen (for most) and food. A compost heap becomes hot (around 60 °C) because the large numbers of micro-organisms respire rapidly and respiration releases heat.

questions.question: Describe how yoghurt is made, giving the reason for each step, and explain how yeast makes bread rise.
questions.expected_answer: Heat milk to about 85 °C to kill unwanted bacteria and change the milk proteins so the yoghurt sets thicker. Cool to about 43 °C so the yoghurt bacteria are not killed. Add a starter of live yoghurt containing the bacteria. Keep warm at about 43 °C for 4 to 8 hours while the bacteria multiply and turn lactose into lactic acid, which thickens the milk proteins, gives the sour taste and preserves it. Refrigerate to slow the bacteria. Bread: yeast (a single-celled fungus) breaks down sugar in the warm dough, releasing carbon dioxide and a little alcohol; the carbon dioxide forms bubbles trapped in the dough so it rises; baking kills the yeast, drives off the alcohol and sets the bubbles.

questions.question: Describe the discovery of penicillin and explain how it works and why it is useless against viruses. Name two other useful roles of micro-organisms.
questions.expected_answer: In 1928 Alexander Fleming noticed that a Penicillium mould contaminating a dish of bacteria had killed the bacteria around it; he named the substance penicillin. Florey and Chain purified it around 1940 and it was mass-produced by 1944; the three shared the Nobel Prize in 1945. Penicillin is an antibiotic that stops bacteria building their cell walls so they burst; human cells have no cell walls so are unharmed; viruses have no cell walls and live inside our cells, so it has no effect on them. Other roles: nitrogen-fixing bacteria in legume root nodules turn nitrogen from the air into compounds plants use; microbes in the rumen digest cellulose for cattle; gut bacteria make vitamin K; bacteria treat sewage; bacteria produce biogas; genetically modified bacteria make insulin; bacteria clean up oil spills.
